column3: It repeats the misguidance formula and closes every available path, closely matching the focus's lack of a protector and return route.
It describes people led astray and astraying others from the level path, supplying the antecedent of the focus's final loss of direction.
Its repeated claims of seeing concern contemptuous social judgment, not the late sight of punishment or an unavailable return.
It pairs the Day's flight with God's misguidance and the absence of any guide, a close parallel to the focus's abandonment and no protector.
The immediate continuation shows the wrongdoers exposed to the punishment they now see, then names their lasting loss and punishment.
The promised inheritance of land after oppressors does not clarify misguidance, seeing punishment, or a request to return.
It exactly states that one whom God leaves astray has no guide, directly reinforcing the focus's closed post-misguidance condition.
It makes present blindness culminate in greater error of path in the Hereafter, explaining the focus's final inability to find a way back.
It shows people seeing a sign yet responding with mockery, a useful contrast to the focus's compelled recognition only after punishment is seen.
Wrongdoers see the punishment and conceal regret while judgment is executed justly, closely paralleling the focus's late recognition.
It warns of a day God will not turn back, when neither refuge nor denial remains, directly clarifying the futile request for return.
Its claimed absence of liability toward others uses path language in a financial-ethical setting, not a route back after judgment.
Those in error finally see the promised punishment or the Hour and learn their true position, matching the focus's sequence of misguidance and late sight.
The immediate continuation addresses turning away from the message, but does not itself develop the final lack of protection or return.
The false promises of hypocrites concern failed political support, without the focus's misguidance, punishment, or return request.
It joins injustice with God's not guiding wrongdoers, supplying a direct moral counterpart to the focus's divine misguidance.
It contrasts inner dispositions with the one better guided on the path, providing a general account of the direction the focus says has been lost.
It concerns obstructing God's way and forcing religious reversal, rather than the wrongdoers' inability to return after punishment.
It ends with the same misguidance formula and no guide, while situating it within accountable deeds and diversion from the path.
The distribution of children and barrenness does not bear on the focus's judgment, protection, or return imagery.
It warns that obedience to others can turn believers back after faith, a living counterpart to the focus's impossible request to return.
It explicitly says that one God leaves astray will find neither a protecting ally nor a directing guide, nearly matching the focus's wording.
The invitation to the path of right guidance supplies the positive alternative to the focus's condition of being left without direction.
It shows that repentance may follow punishment in a different setting, contrasting with the focus's final scene where no authorized return is available.
Authorities see the signs yet imprison Joseph, showing sight that fails to produce timely right judgment; the focus reverses this with too-late sight.
Divine ownership and the granting of children do not clarify misguidance, punishment, or return.
It describes obstructing God's way, a broad precursor to loss of direction but not the focus's final condition.
It denies any protector or helper apart from God, directly echoing the focus's declaration that the misguided have no protector.
The warning against an evil path concerns conduct before wrongdoing, not a route of return after judgment.
It affirms the return to God and identifies the excessive as companions of the Fire, strongly framing the focus's requested but unavailable return.
It repeats that apart from God people have neither protector nor helper, a direct parallel to the focus's no-protector statement.
It places disputants about the Hour in far error while believers know it is true, supplying the judgment horizon that the focus makes visible.
It distinguishes truthful inner perception from denied sight, contrasting with the focus's sight of punishment that arrives only after certainty is forced.
It directly combines wrongdoers seeing punishment, concealed regret, and consequences for their deeds, closely paralleling the focus's late realization.
It asks whether anyone can guide the blind who do not see, explaining why outward observation does not itself reverse misguidance.
Its hypothetical arrival of punishment or the Hour asks whom people would call, but does not develop the focus's final loss of a return route.
It states that belief no longer benefits people once they see God's punishment, directly clarifying why the focus's late response cannot restore the past.
The nearby sign in stilled ships supplies only general surah context and no direct account of punishment, protection, or return.
It contrasts those who judge the coming event far off with the focus's point at which it becomes undeniably seen.
The immediate passage denies any protector or helper apart from God, directly reinforcing the focus's lack of a protector after misguidance.
Those in punishment admit that obedience to leaders led them away from the path, providing a concrete account of the focus's misguidance.
The deniers ask whether they will be returned to their former state, a close verbal counterpart to the focus's desperate request for return.
It says wrongdoers are allies of one another while God is protector of the mindful, sharpening the focus's distinction between false and real protection.
The same surah links unauthorized religious authority with painful punishment for wrongdoers, supplying a local antecedent to the focus's scene.
Seeing even an atom's weight of evil gives a broad final-accountability parallel, without the focus's misguidance or plea to return.
What God withholds cannot be released by anyone after Him, a close structural parallel to the focus's irreversible loss after divine judgment.
It uses God's path for migration and promised provision, not the wrongdoers' unavailable avenue of return.
The unseen armies contrast visible and invisible aid, but do not explain the late sight of punishment or lack of protection.
It contrasts God, who guides to truth, with alleged partners unable to guide unless guided, directly illuminating the focus's divine misguidance and no protector.
It identifies God alone as the true protector, directly clarifying why no alternative protector remains in the focus.
The enduring road of a destroyed people is a geographical reference without a relevant return or judgment relation.
It names wrongdoers who knowingly reject God's signs, supplying the culpable rejection that precedes the focus's final punishment.
It depicts people being turned from the path while believing themselves guided, a direct account of the misguidance exposed in the focus.
It asks what discourse people will believe after God's signs, but does not add a focused relation to final punishment or return.
Persistent doubt after clear signs is followed by God's misguidance of the excessive doubter, closely matching the focus's causal condition.
The statement of God's subtle provision does not clarify the focus's misguidance, punishment, or unavailable return.
The question about named idols provides no material link to the focus's final scene.
When God wills harm, it cannot be turned back and people have no protector apart from Him, closely paralleling both closed elements of the focus.
Created earthly paths are a broad positive contrast to the focus's lost path, without its judgment setting.
The Paradise description of not seeing sun or bitter cold does not clarify the focus's sight of punishment.
It commands response before a day that God will not turn back, directly parallel to the focus's futile search for a way of return.
God's mercy after despair and His protectorship offer only a broad local contrast to the focus's final withdrawal of protection.
The announced punishment is explicitly not to be turned back, directly clarifying the irreversible outcome behind the focus's request.
The battle participants ask whether they possess any control over the matter, a distant parallel to the focus's powerless post-event question.
Wrongdoers' false description of the Messenger is rejection language, but it does not develop late punishment or a return route.
The prayer asks to be shown the promised punishment, supplying an anticipatory counterpart to the focus's actual sight of it.
After judgment Satan disowns his followers, denies mutual rescue, and leaves wrongdoers in painful punishment, closely reinforcing the focus's lack of help.
The surah's warning of the indisputable Day of Gathering and division between Garden and Blaze frames the final scene in the focus.
It warns that following disbelievers turns believers back on their heels as losers, a moral counterpart to the focus's now-impossible reversal.
The absence of a heavenly army after the messenger's death does not clarify protection, punishment seen, or return.
In the Fire people wish they had obeyed God and the Messenger, a close late-regret parallel to the focus's request for reversal.
The rain causing the earth to become green has no relation to the focus's final judgment scene.
It states that God does not guide wrongdoers, providing a concise moral parallel to the focus's misguidance formula.
It says God guides to Himself those who turn back, supplying the timely positive alternative to the focus's belated desire to return.
The prayer asks to be shown what the deniers are promised, usefully anticipating the focus's sight of punishment.
The poets' failure to do what they say does not clarify misguidance, punishment, or an avenue of return.
The earth's broad roads are physical paths and only a remote contrast to the focus's unavailable path of return.
The rhetorical question about belief after revelation has no specific relation to the focus's final scene.
It directly says that the observer will see criminals chained on that Day, closely matching the focus's visualized judgment of wrongdoers.
The local command to call, remain upright, and recognize the final return to God gives the positive surah alternative to the focus's misdirection.
Joseph's brothers plan wrongdoing while assuming they can become righteous afterward, a limited contrast to the focus's futile post-deed reversal.
Its oppression and fighting setting is a distant background parallel, without the focus's misguidance or final request for return.
Its theological use of seeking a way to the Throne does not clarify a way of return after punishment.
God's hearing and seeing reassure Moses and Aaron, but do not bear on the wrongdoers' late sight or lack of protection.
The oppressed ask God for a protector and helper, a strong counter-scene that defines the protection absent from the misguided in the focus.
The modes of divine communication do not clarify misguidance, punishment, or return.
Seeing great signs is an earlier revelatory sight, not the compelled sight of punishment in the focus.
Repeated rejection of clear proofs leads to sealed hearts, supplying a close account of the hardened misguidance preceding final punishment.
The declaration of God's transcendence does not materially clarify the focus's judgment or return request.
It presents deviation as the only alternative to the recognized truth, directly framing the focus's condition of being left astray.
Its ritual rules for pilgrimage and return have no relevant relation to a return after final punishment.
Messengers warn so people have no excuse before God, explaining why the focus's late recognition cannot reopen the time for response.
Inheritance allocations do not clarify the focus's misguidance, punishment, or return imagery.
A wrongdoer is punished and then returned to his Lord for a harsher punishment, providing a related final-return and judgment sequence.
Divine knowledge and later reporting of deeds supply only a broad accountability frame, without the focus's visual or return language.
Unseen divine aid and God's sight of deeds concern believers under attack, not the wrongdoers' sight of punishment.
The isolated description of dark smoke-shadow adds no focused connection to the requested return or protection.
It emphatically states that people will see Hell, directly paralleling the focus's decisive sight of punishment.
The question for a healer at death does not clarify misguidance, final punishment, or a route of return.
Earlier peoples receive clear signs yet reject the messengers in doubt, supplying the pre-judgment refusal that makes the focus's late recognition meaningful.
Those who follow false leaders see the punishment, disown one another, and wish for a return to disassociate themselves, directly paralleling the focus's late, futile reversal.
Those cursed by God are told they will find no helper, reinforcing the focus's denial of effective protection after divine judgment.
It asks whether anyone can guide one whom God has led astray and declares that no path can be found for such a person, closely matching the focus's closed condition.
It states that an evildoer will find neither protector nor helper apart from God, directly parallel to the focus's no-protector clause.
It declares that for one whom God leaves astray, no way can be found, a direct lexical and conceptual parallel to the focus's unavailable return path.
It says wrongdoers will have no helpers after their final loss, supporting the focus's denial of protection in punishment.
Those standing before the Fire wish they could be returned so as not to deny their Lord's signs, one of the closest parallels to the focus's request for return after seeing punishment.
It answers the preceding wish to return by exposing it as belated and unreliable, clarifying why such a post-exposure reversal cannot reopen the prior moral state.
God's leaving people in error is set against His guidance, supplying a close account of the misguidance premise in the focus.
The warning describes people who will have no protector or intercessor apart from God, reinforcing the focus's absence of a protecting ally.
When the final outcome arrives, people ask for intercessors or a return so they can act differently, directly matching the focus's late request for a way back.
It explicitly says that no one can guide whom God leaves astray and that such people are left wandering, closely paralleling the focus's opening condition.
It states that no one can remove harm God decrees, providing a direct irreversibility counterpart to the focus's vain hope of escape.
It warns that turning toward wrongdoers leaves people with no protectors besides God and then no help, reinforcing the focus's protection language.
It contrasts divine misguidance with guidance for those who turn back, supplying the timely alternative to the focus's belated wish to return.
It warns that following desires after knowledge leaves no protector against God, closely matching the focus's no-protector outcome.
When punishment arrives, wrongdoers ask for delay so they may respond to the call, directly paralleling the focus's too-late request for reversal.
It says that one whom God leaves astray has no guide and no helpers, joining both central elements of the focus in one statement.
On the Day a witness is raised from every community, disbelievers are not permitted to make excuses, clarifying the finality of the focus's scene.
When wrongdoers see the punishment, it is neither lightened nor delayed, directly explaining why the focus's request cannot yield a return.
It says those God leaves astray have no protectors besides Him and portrays their final blind, deaf, and mute gathering toward Hell.
It assigns all protection and judgment to God alone and denies that He shares His rule, supporting the focus's exclusion of any alternative protector.
The criminals see the Fire, know they will fall into it, and find no escape from it, directly paralleling the focus's sight of punishment and closed route.
The promised punishment comes suddenly, cannot be repelled, and receives no delay, strongly supporting the focus's irreversible final moment.
Whenever those in the Fire seek to leave it, they are returned to it, a concrete counterpart to the focus's denied avenue of return.
At death, the wrongdoer asks to be sent back, directly matching the focus's post-realization desire to return.
It denies the requested return by placing an intervening barrier until resurrection, directly clarifying the closure implied in the focus.
Those who reject the message will not believe until they see the painful punishment, closely framing the focus's too-late sight.
It distinguishes the Prophet's inability to guide whom he loves from God's sole guidance, clarifying the divine agency behind the focus's misguidance formula.
It denies any escape from God and any protector or helper besides Him, directly reinforcing the focus's closed protection language.
It asks who can guide one whom God has led astray and declares that such people have no helpers, closely matching the focus's premise and consequence.
It says people have no protector or intercessor apart from God, a close support for the focus's no-protector clause.
The guilty say, after seeing and hearing the truth, that they should be sent back to do good, one of the clearest parallels to the focus's late return request.
It asks who can protect people from what God wills for them, reinforcing the focus's denial of any effective protection against divine judgment.
The condemned are told they will find neither protector nor helper, directly supporting the focus's final absence of a protecting ally.
It contrasts the one whose evil is made appealing with those God guides or leaves astray, supplying a nearby account of the misguidance exposed at judgment.
The people of the Fire ask to be brought out so they can do good rather than their former deeds, directly paralleling the focus's plea for return.
It explicitly states that one whom God leaves astray has no guide, closely repeating the focus's opening divine-misguidance formula.
It states that no one can mislead whom God guides and no one can guide whom He leaves astray, directly clarifying the focus's irreversible loss of direction.
It assigns all intercession to God, reinforcing the focus's exclusion of an independent protector or means of rescue.
The soul regrets its neglect toward God after the fact, supplying the interior regret that the focus externalizes as a request to return.
The soul wishes for another turn so it can become a doer of good, a direct verbal and moral parallel to the focus's desire for return.
After admitting their disbelief, people ask whether there is any way out, closely paralleling the focus's question about an avenue of return.
It says that those who reject God's signs have Hell before them and that what they acquired and took as protectors will not avail them, directly reinforcing the focus's failed-protection scene.
It asks who can guide the one God has left astray after knowledge, directly paralleling the focus's opening and its final inability to recover direction.
It warns that one who does not answer God's caller cannot escape Him and will have no protectors besides Him, closely matching the focus's closed outcome.
It distinguishes God as protector of believers from disbelievers who have no protector, supporting the focus's no-protector distinction.
It denies the hypocrites and disbelievers any protector or helper on the final Day, directly supporting the focus's hopeless judgment setting.
At the approach of death, a person asks for a brief delay to give and become righteous, a related but less exact instance of too-late reversal.
When the promised punishment is seen approaching, the faces of disbelievers are distressed, closely supporting the focus's visualized encounter with punishment.
It declares that none can protect from God and that no refuge can be found apart from Him, directly reinforcing the focus's no-protector and no-way language.
At the final upheaval, the human being asks where there is an escape, a direct counterpart to the focus's search for a way back.
It answers that there is no refuge, directly clarifying the focus's unavailable route after punishment is seen.
The disbeliever's wish to become dust at the near punishment supplies a final-regret counterpart to the focus's impossible return request.
